newsitem.title: CROATIA: U.S. arms shipments to Bosnia finally begin.
newsitem.headline: U.S. arms shipments to Bosnia finally begin.

text.p: U.S. heavy weaponry shipments to the Balkans began on Thursday, a year to the day after the end of the Bosnian war for which the Sarajevo government so desperately needed them.

The ship "American Condor" began off-loading its cargo in the Croatian port of Ploce as part of $100 million worth of U.S. military aid to make Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation the battlefield equal of the country's rival Serb republic.
"Throughout the war, Federation forces were unable to bring to Bosnia the heavy weapons needed for adequate defence," U.S. Special Envoy James Pardew said in a shipboard ceremony.

The delivery was long delayed after Washington insisted the Federation's Moslem Deputy Defense Minister, Hasan Cengic, be sacked because of his alleged close ties with Iran, a nation Washington accuses of sponsoring state terrorism.
The American Condor idled in the Adriatic for nearly a month at a reported cost of $50,000 a day until the dispute was resolved. Cengic was finally removed on Tuesday.

"The purpose of the Train and Equip Progamme is to prevent war by creating a military balance in Bosnia," said Pardew. "If deterrence fails, the Federation must be capable of defending its people and its territory."

Pardew said the American Condor would unload 45 tanks, 80 armoured personnel carriers, 15 utility helicopters, 45,000 rifles, ammunition, 5,000 pieces of communications gear and other related equipment.

Tanks and armoured personnel carriers painted a dull green were chained to the decks of the ship in tight rows and columns. Wooden crates of arms and ammunition were stacked higher than a man in many places.
The United Arab Emirates has also donated tanks and artillery, already aboard a ship docked in Ploce, and artillery and air defence weapons from Egypt is due soon.
The total value of the Train and Equip programme is expected to exceed $400 million.
Federation Vice-President Ejup Ganic took delivery of the military cargo and remembered the years when Bosnia's Moslems fought for their lives, handicapped by a U.N. arms embargo.
Small arms and ammunition were smuggled into Bosnia in violation of the embargo, but with great difficulty. The Bosnian army captured the only heavy weapons they had.
"In the past when Bosnia received arms it was a science fiction story," Ganic recalled. "We had to cross four blockades to get anything, even a small package, inside."
The Dayton peace agreement which ended Bosnia's 43-month war was initialled a year ago on November 21, 1995.

Dayton's military annexe allowed for the Train and Equip Programme in the context of overall arms reduction in Bosnia and on condition the country's Moslem and Croat armies combine into a single federation force.

Arms reductions being supervised by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe are behind schedule and difficulties in forming the Federation army and its command structure delayed the off-loading of the American Condor.
There was irony aplenty in Thursday's arms shipment.
Although Washington called for the lifting of the U.N. arms embargo against Bosnia often during the war, it was Iran which acted and supplied the Moslems when they were at their neediest.
The U.S. looked the other way then and has spent much of the past year trying to wean Sarajevo away from Tehran.

Only last week U.S. troops on NATO peace duty in Bosnia confiscated hundreds of assault rifles and tonnes of ammunition from a Bosnian Army unit and destroyed them as a punishment for an alleged violation of the Dayton peace agreement.
The U.S. rifles and ammunition off-loaded in Ploce on Thursday will replace what the U.S. destroyed in that raid.
